title: PKK Peace Bill Reaches Parliament With 360 Votes — Enough for a Constitutional Referendum, Hormuz Deal Nears, Black Sea Crisis Deepens
subhead: Turkey's Kurdish peace framework law was formally submitted to parliament with 360 lawmaker signatures — the exact number needed to trigger a constitutional referendum, fueling speculation Erdogan is trading peace for a path to a third term. Meanwhile, an Iran-Oman Hormuz deal appears imminent, and Black Sea drone attacks on Turkish-linked shipping are disrupting global commodity flows.

sections.heading: PKK Peace Bill Submitted to Parliament With 360 Signatures
sections.body:
Turkey's ruling AKP and its allies formally submitted the 'Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration' to parliament's Justice Committee on Wednesday, marking the first time legislation has been introduced following direct negotiations with imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan. The bill was signed by 360 of 592 lawmakers — including deputies from the AKP, MHP, pro-Kurdish DEM Party, CHP, New Path Party, and HÜDA PAR, according to Bianet and AFP.

The number is significant: 360 is the minimum needed to trigger a constitutional referendum, and 400 would allow parliament to amend the constitution outright without a public vote. Erdogan's current term expires in May 2028, and he is constitutionally barred from seeking re-election. The Al-Monitor analysis notes that Wednesday's show of support suggests Erdogan could corral enough votes to secure a referendum to change that — and if 400 lawmakers back the peace bill, he may not even need one.

The bill establishes a staggered legal mechanism: investigations and trials for PKK membership, leadership, propaganda, and financing offenses would be deferred for five to ten years depending on severity. Intentional homicides are excluded, as are pre-2005 offenses carrying life sentences. A board chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz — including the foreign, interior, justice, and defense ministers, plus intelligence and national security officials — would oversee disarmament and dissolution. A 17-member parliamentary monitoring commission would follow up with further legislation.

PKK members would have six months to submit reintegration applications after the National Security Council formally certifies the group's dissolution. The fast-track procedure means the bill could pass as early as this weekend or early next week.

The Yeni (New) Party — Ozgur Özel's splinter from CHP, now the main opposition with 91 seats — did not sign the bill and has not yet announced its stance, according to the Bangkok Post. The nationalist İYİ Party opposes the process and refused to sign. Özel is expected to vote in favor when the bill reaches the floor, in a bid to maintain bridges with Kurdish voters, Al-Monitor reports.

Öcalan signaled support from his prison cell on Monday, calling the legislation 'a key' that would 'crack open the door' to further reforms such as constitutionally enshrined language rights, while noting it left much unaddressed. MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli — who initiated the peace process in October 2024 — went further on Wednesday, calling for the release of both Öcalan and former HDP leader Selahattin Demirtaş, who has been jailed since 2016 on terrorism charges the European Court of Human Rights has ruled were politically motivated.
sections.whyItMatters: The 360-signature threshold is not coincidental — it is the exact number required to call a constitutional referendum that could allow Erdogan to run for a third term. The peace process and Erdogan's political survival are now formally entwined. Whether the bill genuinely resolves the Kurdish question or merely instrumentalizes it depends entirely on what follow-up legislation and constitutional reforms follow.

sections.heading: Hormuz Deal Inches Closer as Iran-Oman Draft Nears Completion
sections.body:
Iran said Wednesday it is in the 'final stage' of drafting an agreement with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and US President Donald Trump said a deal could be announced this week. Regional officials told the AP that Iranian and Omani negotiators have finalized a draft that awaits approval from Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since being reportedly wounded in the war's opening strikes.

The proposed arrangement would have ships enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through an Omani-controlled route, with service fees charged for security and maritime environmental preservation, according to two regional officials briefed on the talks. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said a joint statement would be issued 'if certain parties do not obstruct this process' — a veiled reference to the US.

The US has strongly opposed any arrangement allowing Iran to charge fees for Hormuz transit, which would effectively cement Tehran's control over the waterway. Trump told reporters on Tuesday: 'It could happen. Tomorrow or the next day. A lot of progress has been made.' Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged progress but said no final agreement has been reached. Vice President JD Vance called the negotiations 'messy' and described Iranians as 'extraordinarily difficult people.'

Brent crude hovered around $80 per barrel — well below conflict highs but still elevated — as markets priced in the possibility of a deal while hedging against last-minute breakdowns.
sections.whyItMatters: A Hormuz deal would dramatically ease global energy pressure and Turkey's own import bill, but the fee-based arrangement Iran is pushing would set a precedent for state control over international waterways. For Turkey, which imports virtually all its oil and gas, reopening Hormuz would be an economic relief — but any Iranian-enforced transit fees would still raise costs above pre-war levels.

sections.heading: Black Sea Drone Attacks Disrupt Turkish Shipping
sections.body:
A surge in drone and missile attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea is disrupting global grain and oil supplies and has forced at least two major shipping operators — Russia's state-controlled Fesco and Turkey's private operator Kalyon — to suspend sailings, according to TradeWinds and Reuters. Ukraine struck Turkish-linked vessels in the Black Sea earlier this week, Reuters reported.

Turkey's Foreign Ministry warned on Tuesday that escalation in the Black Sea could have far-reaching consequences, including for global food security, after drone attacks struck two Turkish-linked cargo ships. The ministry called for de-escalation and respect for freedom of navigation, dpa reported.

The attacks turn the Black Sea into the latest strategic trade chokepoint under pressure, alongside the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Reuters noted. Global supplies of grain and oil are being squeezed across multiple simultaneous disruptions.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is both a Black Sea coastal state and a major grain importer. Attacks on Turkish-linked shipping in waters Turkey considers strategically vital create a direct national security pressure that complements the Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions. The cumulative effect of three simultaneous chokepoint crises pushes Turkey's import costs higher and complicates its balancing act between Russia and Ukraine.

sections.heading: Cyprus: Leaders to Meet August 26 as Peace Process Gains Momentum
sections.body:
President Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman will meet under UN auspices on August 26 at 4pm, Cyprus Mail reported. The meeting was agreed by negotiators on Wednesday and follows UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' visit to the island last week, which produced a consensus among the three guarantor powers — Turkey, Greece, and the UK — for a new expanded conference.

AK Party spokesman Ömer Çelik confirmed last week that Cyprus 'will continue to be discussed on the basis of diplomacy and the United Nations' parameters,' marking a notable shift toward engagement with the UN framework.

The meeting comes amid a leadership transition in the Turkish Cypriot community: former leader Ersin Tatar on Wednesday accused Turkish opposition leader Özgur Özel of having 'unduly interfered' in last year's Turkish Cypriot election, claiming Özel campaigned for Erhurman. The irony is that AK Party figures — including Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, former interior minister Süleyman Soylu, and former footballer Mesut Özil — had also traveled to Cyprus to campaign for Tatar.
sections.whyItMatters: The August 26 meeting is a concrete step toward reviving Cyprus negotiations after years of stalemate. Turkey's willingness to engage within UN parameters — and its acceptance of Erhurman's election — signals a pragmatic shift, especially as Ankara seeks international legitimacy alongside the PKK peace process.

sections.heading: Israel-Hezbollah Ceasefire Fraying as Rome Talks Interrupted
sections.body:
The shaky Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire came under strain on Wednesday. Israel's military issued an evacuation warning for residents of the southern Lebanese village of Mansouri — the first such warning in weeks — and then carried out 'precise strikes' in southern Lebanon, claiming response to a 'blatant violation' of the ceasefire that had largely held since June 20, the Jerusalem Post reported.

The escalation came as Lebanese and Israeli negotiators were meeting in Rome for a second day to discuss implementation of a deal under which Israeli forces are supposed to withdraw from occupied areas in southern Lebanon in exchange for Hezbollah's disarmament. A State Department official said the talks ended early 'due to events on the ground' but could continue Thursday, adding the discussions 'were extremely productive,' according to the New York Times.

For Turkey, the fraying ceasefire complicates its diplomatic positioning. Erdogan has repeatedly positioned himself as a champion of Palestinian and Lebanese causes, and any return to full-scale Israel-Hezbollah fighting would increase domestic political pressure on his government while diverting international attention from the PKK peace process and Hormuz negotiations.
sections.whyItMatters: A renewed Israel-Hezbollah conflict would dominate the regional agenda and draw Turkey back into the Israel-Gaza-Lebanon rhetorical arena, potentially distracting from the carefully managed PKK peace rollout. Erdogan's domestic credibility with his conservative base depends in part on his stance on Lebanon, but he needs international goodwill for the Kurdish process.

sections.heading: Salah Arrives in Trabzon as Turkey's Sports-Soft-Power Play Continues
sections.body:
Mohamed Salah completed his transfer to Trabzonspor on Wednesday, arriving to a hero's welcome from an estimated 25,000 fans at the club's stadium. The Egyptian winger, a free agent after leaving Liverpool, signed a reported two-year deal with the Turkish club, according to Yahoo Sports and Middle East Eye.

While primarily a football story, Salah's arrival in Turkey is significant in context: it brings one of the Arab world's most recognizable public figures to a Turkish club at a moment when Erdogan is courting regional influence and seeking to burnish Turkey's image as a welcoming destination for the Muslim world's biggest names. The images of fans chanting 'Allahu Akbar' as Salah was unveiled will resonate across the region.
sections.whyItMatters: Salah's transfer to Trabzonspor is a soft-power moment for Turkey at a time when Ankara is simultaneously pursuing a Kurdish peace process and seeking regional diplomatic capital. In the intersection of sports, politics, and identity, the imagery of the Arab world's biggest football star embraced by Turkish fans reinforces Turkey's cultural pull in the Middle East.

bottomLine: The PKK peace bill reaching parliament with 360 signatures — the precise number needed for a constitutional referendum — turns what was billed as a Kurdish reconciliation process into an implicit vehicle for Erdogan's political future. The bill is likely to pass within days, but the real test will be whether follow-up legislation on language rights, political participation, and Öcalan's status matches the promise. Regionally, a Hormuz deal appears closer than it has in months, which would ease Turkey's energy import burden, even as Black Sea drone attacks on Turkish-linked ships create a new threat to its trade routes. The Cyprus process is quietly gaining momentum with an August 26 leaders' meeting, and the Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire is fraying — a combination that keeps Turkey's diplomatic plate full at exactly the moment it is pursuing its most consequential domestic reform in decades.
sources: Al-Monitor, Anadolu Agency, Bangkok Post (AFP), Bianet, Cyprus Mail, Reuters, TradeWinds, Washington Post, Yahoo Sports, Middle East Eye, dpa, Jerusalem Post, New York Times, CNBC TV18, AsiaOne, TASS
